questions.question: What's the difference between Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment/Delivery?
options: CI automatically builds and tests every push; CD automatically packages/ships the result if CI passes
CI only applies to Docker, CD only applies to .NET
questions.explanation: CI catches broken code early via automated build+test on every push. CD extends that by automatically delivering the working result (e.g., a Docker image) once CI succeeds — together forming an automated pipeline.

questions.question: What does `needs: build-and-test` on the image-push job accomplish?
options: The push job only runs if the build-and-test job succeeded — preventing a broken build from being packaged and pushed
It makes the jobs run in parallel
questions.explanation: This dependency is what turns several independent jobs into a real PIPELINE — a failure upstream (failing tests) automatically blocks everything downstream (pushing an image), with no manual intervention needed.

questions.question: Where should Docker Hub credentials used by a GitHub Actions workflow be stored?
options: Hardcoded directly in the workflow YAML file
As GitHub repository secrets, referenced via ${{ secrets.NAME }} — never committed to source
In a comment in the Dockerfile
In an environment variable set on the developer's own laptop
questions.explanation: Same principle as Module 7's JWT signing key — real secrets belong in a secrets manager (here, GitHub's repo secrets), never committed to source control where anyone with repo access (or a public repo, anyone at all) could read them.

questions.question: What happens on GitHub when `dotnet test` fails inside a workflow run?
options: The job (and the overall run) is marked failed, visible on the PR — and can block merging if a branch protection rule requires the check to pass
The workflow automatically fixes the failing test
questions.explanation: A failed step fails the job, which fails the run — visible as a red X on the PR/commit. Combined with a branch protection rule, this can literally prevent merging code with failing tests.

questions.question: Each GitHub Actions job runs on a fresh, temporary virtual machine, with nothing persisting from previous runs unless explicitly cached or saved.
questions.explanation: `runs-on: ubuntu-latest` provisions a clean VM for that job. This is why workflows explicitly check out code, restore dependencies, etc. every time — nothing is assumed to already be there from a previous run.
